corpus_definition: A habit or tradition shared by a group of people.

forms.definition: a way of behaving that people in a place have followed for a long time
forms.example: It is an old custom in Uzbekistan to offer guests tea first.

syn.note: Very close; tradition often sounds older and more important.
A usual way of doing something, often in a job or religion.
A rule of behaviour that most people accept; more formal.
Related: a habit is usually one person's; a custom belongs to a group.
Related: a fixed set of actions, often at a ceremony.

forms.definition: the place at a border where officials check your bags
forms.example: We waited an hour at customs at Tashkent airport.
forms.note: Belongs to custom = tax on goods brought into a country, not a group's tradition. Always plural in this meaning.

forms.definition: to make someone used to something so it feels normal
forms.example: It took a few weeks to accustom myself to the cold winters.
forms.note: Most often used as 'be/get accustomed to something'.

syn.note: Related: you change yourself to fit a new situation.
Related: you learn about something so it is no longer new. British spelling: familiarise.
Very formal, mostly in science writing.

forms.definition: to change something so it fits what one person wants
forms.example: You can customize the phone with your own colours and sounds.
forms.note: Belongs to custom = made for one buyer (custom-made), not a group's tradition. British spelling: customise.

forms.definition: usual or traditional in a particular place or group
forms.example: It is customary to take off your shoes before entering a home.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word; customary is more formal.
Done in the same way for a long time.
Related: what people expect; not always about tradition.
Related: done again and again, often by one person.

ant.note: Not done often; different from what people expect.

forms.definition: familiar with something, so it does not feel strange
forms.example: After a month in London, I was accustomed to the rain.
forms.note: Used as 'be accustomed to + noun / -ing'.

syn.note: Easy and very common: 'be used to something'.
Related: you know it well.

forms.definition: in the usual or traditional way of a group
forms.example: Plov is customarily cooked by men at big family events.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word.
Done this way for a long time.
Related: what usually happens, not always a tradition.

people.definition: a person who buys things from a shop or business
people.example: The shop was full of customers on Saturday.
people.note: Belongs to an old meaning of custom = buying regularly at one shop, not a group's tradition.

context.text: In Uzbekistan it is a custom to offer guests tea first. Visitors soon become accustomed to it, and it is customary to accept at least one cup.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: customs (border), customize and customer belong to other meanings of custom and are marked other_meaning.

corpus_definition: Slightly wet in an unpleasant or cold way.

forms.definition: the state of being a little wet, often in an unpleasant way
forms.example: The dampness in the basement made everything smell bad.

syn.note: Small amounts of water in the air or on a surface; neutral, not always unpleasant.
Simple word; can mean very wet too.
Related: water in the air, often used about weather.

forms.definition: a little water in the air or in walls that makes a building unhealthy
forms.example: The old house was cold and full of damp.
forms.note: Mostly British English.

forms.definition: to make something a little wet
forms.example: Dampen the cloth before you clean the table.
forms.note: Also means 'to make a feeling weaker': 'The rain didn't dampen our spirits.'

syn.note: Very close; a little more formal.
Easy word; can mean making something very wet.

forms.definition: a little wet, in a way that feels cold or unpleasant
forms.example: My shoes were still damp from the rain.

syn.note: A little wet, often in a good way (moist cake); damp is usually unpleasant.
Related: wet can mean covered in a lot of water.
Related: used for hot air or weather with a lot of water in it.
Related: very wet and soft, often about food or ground.

forms.note: No common adverb. 'Damply' exists but is very rare; learners say 'in a damp way' or use the adjective.

context.text: After three days of rain, the walls of our flat in Bukhara felt damp. My mother opened all the windows because dampness is bad for your health.

reviewer_note: damp vs wet vs moist: damp marked as unpleasant; damp noun (British) kept as extra conversion.

corpus_definition: To take action to fix a problem.
particle_note: Not separable: 'deal with the problem' (never 'deal the problem with'). Past: dealt with. Often 'deal with + noun / it / someone'.

relations.note: Very close; also common at work: 'I'll handle it.'
Suggests a hard problem that needs effort.
Informal, mostly British: 'I'll sort it out.'
Formal: start to work on a problem.
Related: control a situation so it doesn't get worse.
To pay no attention to a problem.
To not give something the care or action it needs.

context.text: My manager asked me to deal with an angry customer. I dealt with the problem quickly, and the man left the shop happy.

reviewer_note: Kept only the 'fix a problem' sense; 'deal with = be about (a book deals with war)' is a different meaning, not shown.

forms.definition: a period of ten years
forms.example: My grandparents have lived in Samarkand for five decades.
forms.note: Also used for a group of years like 1990-1999: 'the last decade of the century'.

syn.note: The easy way to say it.
Related: any length of time.
Related: about 25-30 years, the time between parents and children.

forms.note: No verb in this family.
No common adjective. 'Decadent' looks similar but comes from 'decay', not from decade.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: My grandparents have lived in Samarkand for five decades. In the last decade, the city has changed a lot, with new roads and hotels.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; decadent flagged as not_family (false friend from decay).

corpus_definition: to slowly break down and rot over time

forms.definition: the slow process of something breaking down and rotting
forms.example: Sugar causes tooth decay.
forms.note: Also used for buildings or places that slowly get worse: 'the city fell into decay'.

syn.note: Easy word; usually about food, wood or plants.
Scientific word for dead plants or animals breaking down.
Related: when something slowly becomes weaker or worse, not rotting.

forms.definition: to slowly break down and go bad over time
forms.example: The fallen leaves decay on the ground every autumn.

syn.note: Very close and easy; common for food and wood.
Scientific word for dead plants or bodies.
Easy phrase; slowly separate into small parts.
Related: used for food that goes bad.
Related: break into small pieces, often old buildings.

forms.definition: broken down and rotten after a long time
forms.example: The dentist removed a decayed tooth.

syn.note: Easy and common, especially for food.
Scientific; used for dead plants or bodies.

ant.note: New and in good condition, not gone bad.

forms.definition: slowly breaking down and going bad
forms.example: The smell came from decaying fruit under the tree.

forms.note: No adverb in this family.

context.text: Fallen apples decay quickly in the summer heat. The farmer puts the decaying fruit on the compost, and the decay makes the soil rich.

reviewer_note: Noun decay is a conversion; the 'get worse' sense (decline of buildings, cities) only mentioned in a note.

corpus_definition: to make someone believe something that is not true

forms.definition: the act of making someone believe something false
forms.example: The police discovered the deception and arrested the seller.

syn.note: Using clever tricks to fool people.
Related: not telling the truth, in general.
Related: a crime of cheating people, usually for money.
Related: one false statement; easy word.

forms.definition: dishonest behaviour that hides the truth from people
forms.example: Their friendship ended because of his deceit.

syn.note: Not telling the truth; a little more general.

forms.definition: to make someone believe something that is false
forms.example: He tried to deceive his teacher about the missing homework.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Give someone the wrong idea, sometimes not on purpose.
Informal; also used for jokes.
Related: break rules or trick someone to get something.
Related: say something false; deceive can also be done without words.

forms.definition: giving a false idea of what something is really like
forms.example: The photos on the website were deceptive; the hotel was small and old.

syn.note: Very close and common.
Related: not true.

forms.definition: often lying or tricking people to get what you want
forms.example: She was hurt by her deceitful business partner.

syn.note: Easy and very close.

forms.definition: in a way that makes something seem different from how it really is
forms.example: The test looked deceptively easy, but the last questions were hard.
forms.note: Usually before an adjective: deceptively simple, deceptively strong.

syn.note: Similar, but less common.

people.definition: a person who makes others believe things that are false
people.example: Everyone in the village knew he was a deceiver.

context.text: Some online shops deceive buyers with fake photos. The pictures can be deceptive, so read the reviews first and protect yourself from deception.

reviewer_note: No affix claimed on deception/deceptive (decept- is not a word); deceptively = 'misleadingly', not 'dishonestly'.

corpus_definition: acceptable, good enough, or appropriate for a situation

forms.definition: behaviour that is polite, honest and acceptable to most people
forms.example: Have the decency to say sorry when you are late.

syn.note: Correct social behaviour; very formal.
Related: being seen by society as good and proper.
Related: good manners; easy word.

ant.note: Behaviour that shocks people, often about sex or the body.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: good enough or right for a situation
forms.example: Make sure you wear decent clothes to the interview.

syn.note: Good enough; a little more formal.
Fair and not too bad: a reasonable price.
Enough, but not very good; formal.
Related: correct for the situation.
Related: seen as good by other people.

ant.note: Shocking or not acceptable, often about the body.

forms.definition: in an acceptable or good enough way
forms.example: The job is hard, but the workers are paid decently.

syn.note: In the correct way.
Well enough; formal.
Related: fairly well, not too much or too little.

context.text: Aziz finally found a decent job in Tashkent with a decent salary. He dresses decently for work and treats everyone with decency.

reviewer_note: Opposites indecent/indecency/indecently go in ant lists, not forms; 'decent = kind' (a decent person) is close and covered by decency.

corpus_definition: To make something look more beautiful by adding things.

forms.definition: a thing you add to make something look more beautiful
forms.example: We put up lights and paper decorations for the party.
forms.note: Also means a medal given for bravery (another meaning).

syn.note: A small beautiful object, often hung or put on a shelf.
Formal or literary.
Related: the style of colours and furniture in a room. Also written décor.

forms.definition: to make something look more beautiful by adding things to it
forms.example: We will decorate the room with balloons.
forms.note: In British English it also means to paint or paper the walls of a room.

syn.note: Literary or formal.
Formal; mostly in writing.
Make something more beautiful; formal.
Related: add a border or small things to clothes or a tree.
Related: one way to make a room look new.

forms.definition: made to look pretty, not to be useful
forms.example: The plates on the wall are only decorative.

syn.note: Very close; a little more formal.
Related: with a lot of details; informal.
Related: nice to look at; easy word.

ant.note: Made to be useful, not beautiful.

forms.definition: with pretty things added to make it look nicer
forms.example: The bride sat in a beautifully decorated room.

forms.definition: in a way that makes something look pretty
forms.example: The fruit was arranged decoratively on a big plate.

syn.note: Formal and rare.
Related: in a way that is nice to look at.

people.definition: a person whose job is to paint and improve the inside of houses
people.example: We hired a decorator to paint the kitchen.
people.note: American English often says 'interior decorator' for someone who plans the style of a room.

context.text: Before Navruz, we decorate our house with flowers. My sister makes beautiful decorations from coloured paper, and they look very decorative on the white walls.

reviewer_note: Medal sense of decorate/decoration only in a note; decor kept as a related synonym, not a form.

corpus_definition: To make or become smaller in amount or size.

forms.definition: the fact of becoming smaller in number or amount
forms.example: There has been a decrease in the number of road accidents.
forms.note: Stress moves: noun DEcrease, verb deCREASE.

syn.note: Very close; often when someone makes it smaller.
Easy and common, for prices and numbers.
Often a sudden decrease.
A slow decrease over time.
Related: a planned decrease, for example in prices or jobs.

ant.note: Becoming bigger in number or amount.
Going up, for prices and numbers.

forms.definition: to make or become smaller in amount or size
forms.example: We must decrease the amount of salt we eat.

syn.note: Very close; used when someone makes it smaller.
Easy, everyday phrase: 'Prices went down.'
Used for numbers and prices that become smaller.
Often quickly or suddenly.
Slowly over time; a little formal.
Formal; often for pain or risk.

forms.definition: becoming smaller in number or amount over time
forms.example: Decreasing water levels are a problem for farmers near the Aral Sea.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Slowly over a long time.
Related: getting smaller in size.

forms.note: No common adverb. 'Decreasingly' exists but is rare; learners say 'less and less'.

context.text: Traffic in the city centre has decreased since the new metro line opened. This decrease means cleaner air, and the decreasing noise makes life calmer.

reviewer_note: No de- affix claimed (de- is not in the affix table, and 'crease' is unrelated); stress shift noted.

corpus_definition: To win against someone in a game or fight.

forms.definition: the fact of losing a game, fight or war
forms.example: The team was sad after their 2-0 defeat.

syn.note: Easy and common in sport.
Related: a big, heavy defeat; informal.
Related: not succeeding at anything, not only in a game.

ant.note: Winning a game, fight or war.
Easy word for a victory in sport.

forms.definition: to win against someone in a game, fight or war
forms.example: Our players hope to defeat the other team today.

syn.note: Easy and very common in sport.
Win a war and take control of a country or people.
Related: win against a problem or difficulty.
Related: defeat someone very easily and completely.

ant.note: Be beaten by someone: 'We lost to Bunyodkor.'

forms.definition: having lost a game, fight or war
forms.example: The defeated players walked slowly off the field.
forms.note: Also means 'feeling you can't succeed': 'She looked tired and defeated.'

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Related: about a country or people that lost a war.

ant.note: Never beaten: 'The team is undefeated this season.'

forms.note: No adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person who expects to lose or fail before trying
people.example: Don't be such a defeatist; we can still win the match.
people.note: Also an adjective: a defeatist attitude.

context.text: Pakhtakor defeated the visiting team 3-0 last night. After the defeat, the defeated players walked off the field without a word.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR B1); undefeated goes in ant, not forms.
